definition:
The doctrine of leadership and office asks how Christ, the church's only head, governs and cares for his people through human beings. The New Testament describes elders, also called overseers or shepherds, who teach, guard, and care for a congregation, and deacons, who serve its practical needs; behind them stand the apostles, whom Christ appointed as the founding witnesses of his resurrection. Every form of leadership in Scripture is measured by one pattern: Jesus, who said that “even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). Leaders in the church are stewards who answer to Christ for the people entrusted to them, and the people are called to honor and follow them. Christians agree on that much. They differ on how offices are structured (bishops, presbyteries of elders, or the congregation as final earthly authority), and on whether the office of elder or pastor is open to women. Those are second-order questions, matters on which faithful churches divide without dividing the faith.

The Old Testament's most common word for Israel's local leaders is zaqen, ‘elder’, an older man recognized for his standing in family, clan, and town; elders sat in the city gate to settle cases (Ruth 4:2). Its most important image for rulers is the ro‘eh, ‘shepherd’, used of kings, leaders, and God himself. The New Testament uses several words for the same local leaders. Presbyteros means ‘older man’ or ‘elder’ and carries over the synagogue and Old Testament office. Episkopos means ‘overseer’ or ‘guardian’, a word used in the Greek world for supervisors and officials; older English Bibles render it ‘bishop’. Poimēn, ‘shepherd’ (Latin pastor), names the leaders' task in Ephesians 4:11, and the related verb poimainō, ‘to shepherd’, appears in Acts 20:28 and 1 Peter 5:2. Diakonos means ‘servant’ or ‘minister’, used generally of anyone who serves (Paul calls himself and even Christ a diakonos) and more narrowly of the office of deacon (Philippians 1:1). Hebrews calls leaders hēgoumenoi, ‘those who lead’ (Hebrews 13:7, 17), and Paul speaks of those who ‘preside’ or ‘care for’ (proistamenoi, 1 Thessalonians 5:12). Notably, the New Testament never calls a church leader a hiereus, ‘priest’; that word is used of Christ, of Jewish and pagan priests, and of the whole people of God (1 Peter 2:5, 9; Revelation 1:6).
ot:
The Old Testament shows God governing his people through a variety of leaders, and it is candid about their failures. Elders appear early: Moses is sent to “assemble the elders of Israel” in Egypt (Exodus 3:16), and seventy elders ascend Sinai with him (Exodus 24:1). When Moses is exhausted from judging the people alone, his father-in-law Jethro counsels him to appoint “God-fearing, trustworthy men who are averse to dishonest gain” as leaders over smaller groups, “so that your load may be lightened as they share it with you” (Exodus 18:21-22). Leadership is shared, and its first qualifications are character. The same lesson appears when God places his Spirit on seventy elders so that they will help Moses “bear the burden of the people” (Numbers 11:17), and Moses answers a jealous complaint with a longing that points to Pentecost: “I wish that all the LORD's people were prophets” (Numbers 11:29). Before his death Moses prays that the congregation “will not be like sheep without a shepherd” (Numbers 27:17), and God appoints Joshua, “a man with the Spirit in him,” by the laying on of hands (Numbers 27:18), a gesture later used in the church.

Israel had several kinds of office. Priests from the line of Aaron served at the altar and taught the law; Levites assisted them; prophets were raised up by God's direct call to speak his word, sometimes against priests and kings; judges delivered and governed; and kings ruled from David's line. Women appear among those God used to lead and speak: Deborah, “a prophetess,” was “judging Israel” (Judges 4:4), and when the book of the law was found in the temple, King Josiah's officials consulted “Huldah the prophetess” (2 Kings 22:14). Kingship was hedged with limits. Deuteronomy commands that Israel's king write out a copy of the law and read it all his life, so “his heart will not be exalted above his countrymen” (Deuteronomy 17:18-20). When Samuel sought a king among Jesse's sons, God said, “the LORD does not see as man does” (1 Samuel 16:7), and he chose David, of whom the psalm says that God “took him from the sheepfolds” to be “shepherd of His people Jacob” (Psalm 78:70-71).

The history of the monarchy is largely a history of leaders who used the people rather than served them, and the prophets' sharpest words are for them. Micah accuses Jerusalem's leaders who “judge for a bribe” and priests who “teach for a price” (Micah 3:11). Ezekiel 34 is the central text: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who only feed themselves” (Ezekiel 34:2). They have not strengthened the weak or sought the lost, and they have “ruled them with violence and cruelty” (Ezekiel 34:4). God's answer is twofold. He himself will shepherd his flock (Ezekiel 34:11), and he will set over them “one shepherd, My servant David” (Ezekiel 34:23). Jeremiah adds a promise of human shepherds renewed by God: “I will give you shepherds after My own heart, who will feed you with knowledge and understanding” (Jeremiah 3:15). The Old Testament thus ends with a longing both for the true Shepherd-King and for faithful under-shepherds who lead as he does.
nt:
Jesus answers that longing in his own person. He is the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11), and he defines leadership among his followers against every model of domination. When James and John ask for the highest places, he says the rulers of the Gentiles “lord it over them,” but “it shall not be this way among you,” for “whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant” (Mark 10:42-43). At the Last Supper he says, “I am among you as one who serves” (Luke 22:27), and after washing the disciples' feet he tells them, “I have set you an example” (John 13:15). He forbids titles that set some disciples over others: “you have one Teacher, and you are all brothers” (Matthew 23:8). Yet he also appoints leaders. He chooses the Twelve, gives them authority, and after the resurrection restores Peter with a threefold charge: “Feed My lambs,” “Shepherd My sheep,” “Feed My sheep” (John 21:15-17). The apostles hold a unique role as eyewitnesses of the risen Lord and founders of the church (Ephesians 2:20), a role most Christians have understood as unrepeatable in that form.

Acts shows offices emerging to meet needs. When Greek-speaking widows are overlooked in the food distribution, the apostles have the community choose “seven men confirmed to be full of the Spirit and wisdom” (Acts 6:3) so the apostles can give themselves “to prayer and to the ministry of the word” (Acts 6:4); many interpreters see here the pattern for deacons, though the Seven are not called by that title. Elders appear in Jerusalem (Acts 11:30), meet with the apostles at the council (Acts 15:6), and are appointed by Paul and Barnabas “in each church” (Acts 14:23). At Miletus Paul sends for “the elders of the church” of Ephesus (Acts 20:17) and tells them that the Holy Spirit “has made you overseers” and charges them to “Be shepherds of the church of God, which He purchased with His own blood” (Acts 20:28). The same men are called elders, overseers, and shepherds, and Titus 1:5-7 moves from ‘elder’ to ‘overseer’ in the same way. Most scholars conclude that in the New Testament the two words name one office, and that each congregation normally had several elders; the later single bishop over a church or region is a development whose legitimacy the traditions assess differently.

The Pastoral Letters give the fullest instructions. An overseer must be “above reproach, the husband of but one wife, temperate, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach,” not violent, not a lover of money, a good manager of his household, not a recent convert, and well thought of by outsiders (1 Timothy 3:1-7; compare Titus 1:5-9). The phrase ‘husband of one wife’ (literally ‘a one-woman man’) has been read as excluding polygamists, men divorced and remarried, widowers who remarry, or, most commonly today, simply as requiring marital faithfulness. Deacons must be dignified, honest, and tested first (1 Timothy 3:8-13), and 1 Timothy 3:11 speaks of women (Greek gynaikes, which can mean ‘women’ or ‘wives’) in the middle of that list, whom some read as deacons' wives and others as women deacons; Paul commends Phoebe as a diakonos of the church at Cenchreae (Romans 16:1). Elders who lead well, “especially those who work hard at preaching and teaching,” are worthy of “double honor,” including support (1 Timothy 5:17-18), and accusations against them require witnesses (1 Timothy 5:19). Leaders are set apart with prayer and the laying on of hands (Acts 13:3; 1 Timothy 4:14) and are to entrust the teaching to “faithful men who will be qualified to teach others as well” (2 Timothy 2:2). Several texts at the heart of the debate over women in office come from these letters, especially 1 Timothy 2:11-15, alongside 1 Corinthians 11:5, where women pray and prophesy in worship, and 1 Corinthians 14:34-35.

The New Testament gives commands to leaders and to those they lead. Peter, writing “as a fellow elder,” charges elders to shepherd God's flock “not out of compulsion,” “not out of greed,” and “not lording it over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock” (1 Peter 5:1-3), and he reminds them that they serve under “the Chief Shepherd” (1 Peter 5:4), whom he has already called “the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls” (1 Peter 2:25). Hebrews tells believers, “Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they watch over your souls as those who must give an account” (Hebrews 13:17), and Paul asks the Thessalonians to hold such leaders “in highest regard because of their work” (1 Thessalonians 5:13). James warns that teachers “will be judged more strictly” (James 3:1), and John names Diotrephes, “who loves to be first” (3 John 1:9), as the type of the leader gone wrong. Alongside the offices stand the gifts Christ gives the whole body. The ascended Christ gave “apostles,” “prophets,” “evangelists,” and “pastors and teachers” for a purpose: “to equip the saints for works of ministry and to build up the body of Christ” (Ephesians 4:11-12). The leader's work is to make the whole church able to serve.

keyTexts.why: Jethro counsels Moses to share the work of judging with capable, God-fearing, honest men. Leadership is shared, and character comes first.
God puts his Spirit on seventy elders to bear the people's burden with Moses, who wishes that all God's people were prophets.
Israel's king must read God's law all his life so that his heart is not lifted above his brothers. Authority is placed under God's word.
God condemns shepherds who feed themselves, promises to shepherd his flock himself, and promises one shepherd, his servant David.
Jesus rejects the domination of Gentile rulers and defines greatness as service, grounded in his own death as a ransom.
Jesus washes his disciples' feet and gives it as an example. The Lord and Teacher takes the place of a servant.
The risen Jesus restores Peter and charges him to feed and shepherd his sheep. Pastoral leadership flows from love for Christ.
Seven men full of the Spirit and wisdom are chosen to serve tables so the apostles can devote themselves to prayer and the word. Often taken as the pattern for deacons.
Paul addresses the Ephesian elders as overseers and shepherds of the church Christ bought with his blood. The same leaders bear all three titles.
Christ gives apostles, prophets, evangelists, and pastors and teachers to equip the saints for ministry and build up the body.
Instructions for prayer and for women's learning and teaching in the assembly. A central and disputed text in the debate over women in office.
The qualifications for overseers and deacons, overwhelmingly matters of character, household, and reputation.
Titus appoints elders in every town. The passage uses elder and overseer for the same office and stresses holding to sound teaching.
Believers are to obey and submit to leaders who watch over their souls and must give an account to God.
A fellow elder charges elders to shepherd willingly and humbly, as examples rather than lords, under the Chief Shepherd.

history:
The earliest writings after the New Testament show both continuity and change. The Didache (usually dated between about AD 50 and 120) tells churches to appoint for themselves bishops and deacons worthy of the Lord (chapter 15). First Clement, a letter from the church at Rome to the church at Corinth usually dated about 95 to 97, rebukes the Corinthians for removing their presbyters and argues that the apostles appointed bishops and deacons and provided for others to succeed them (chapters 42 and 44); like the New Testament, it seems to use ‘bishop’ and ‘presbyter’ for the same people. In the letters of Ignatius of Antioch, from the early second century, a single bishop presides in each church with a council of presbyters and with deacons, and Ignatius urges the churches to do nothing apart from the bishop. By the late second century Irenaeus could point to lists of bishops succeeding one another in the churches founded by apostles, and the threefold order of bishop, presbyter, and deacon became universal. Jerome (Letter 146 and his commentary on Titus, late fourth century) observed that presbyters and bishops were originally the same and that one presbyter was later set over the others to prevent division, an observation the Reformers often cited. The Council of Nicaea (325) regulated the ordination of bishops (canon 4) and recognized the wider authority of the sees of Alexandria, Rome, and Antioch (canon 6). Gregory the Great's Pastoral Rule (about 590) became the medieval church's handbook for the character and work of those who care for souls.

The Reformation reopened the question. Luther's Address to the Christian Nobility (1520) argued that all the baptized are priests, and that those who hold office in the church do so by the call and commission of the community. Calvin's Ecclesiastical Ordinances for Geneva (1541) set out four offices, pastors, doctors (teachers), elders, and deacons, and Reformed churches developed presbyterian government, in which congregations are ruled by elders and joined in graded assemblies, codified in Scotland's Second Book of Discipline (1578) and in the Westminster standards (1640s). The Church of England kept bishops and the threefold order in its Ordinal (1550), and Richard Hooker's Of the Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity (published from the 1590s) defended episcopacy as ancient and fitting. The Council of Trent (session 23, 1563) affirmed holy orders as a sacrament and the hierarchy of bishops, priests, and ministers. English Separatists, Congregationalists (the Cambridge Platform, 1648), and Baptists (the Second London Confession of 1689, chapter 26) held that each gathered congregation, under Christ, chooses its own elders and deacons. John Wesley, an Anglican priest, set apart Thomas Coke as a superintendent for American Methodists in 1784, and Methodism developed its own form of oversight. The First Vatican Council (1870) defined the primacy and infallibility of the pope, and the Second Vatican Council's Lumen Gentium (1964) taught the collegiality of bishops with the pope and restored the permanent diaconate.

The question of women in church office grew in the modern period. Women preached in early Quaker and Methodist circles, and Margaret Fell's Womens Speaking Justified (1666) defended the practice. Antoinette Brown was ordained by a Congregational church in South Butler, New York, in 1853, and many Holiness and Pentecostal bodies recognized women preachers from their beginnings. Most mainline Protestant churches opened ordination to women during the twentieth century; the Church of England ordained its first women priests in 1994 and consecrated its first woman bishop, Libby Lane, in 2015. The Roman Catholic Church reaffirmed in Pope John Paul II's Ordinatio Sacerdotalis (1994) that priestly ordination is reserved to men, a position the Orthodox churches share, and the Southern Baptist Convention's Baptist Faith and Message (2000) limits the office of pastor to men. Among evangelicals the Council on Biblical Manhood and Womanhood and Christians for Biblical Equality, both founded in 1987, became the main voices of the complementarian and egalitarian positions described below. The site's page on the church sets out episcopal, presbyterian, and congregational government at full strength.

differ.view: Episcopal government (Roman Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, and some Lutheran and Methodist churches)
differ.body: Christ gave his church apostles, and the apostles appointed others to continue their oversight, as Paul did with Timothy and Titus, who themselves appointed elders in many towns. By the early second century each church was led by a bishop with presbyters and deacons, and that threefold order was universal for fifteen centuries. Bishops in succession from the apostles are the visible guardians of the church's unity and teaching, the link that joins each congregation to the church of every age and place. Roman Catholics add that the bishops are united under the successor of Peter; the Orthodox see the bishops as a communion of equals; Anglicans and others keep the historic episcopate as the church's ancient and fitting order. Defenders argue that the pattern of Timothy and Titus, the early and universal practice of the church, and the need for visible unity all support oversight beyond the local congregation.

The New Testament uses ‘elder’ and ‘overseer’ for one office, held by a plurality of men in each church (Acts 14:23; 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5-7). Among the elders, some labor in preaching and teaching and others rule (1 Timothy 5:17), which grounds the distinction between teaching elders (ministers) and ruling elders. Local churches are not isolated: as the apostles and elders met in Jerusalem to decide a question for all the churches (Acts 15), congregations are joined in graded assemblies of elders (session, presbytery, synod or general assembly) to which appeals may be made. Defenders hold that this order follows the New Testament most closely, guards against the tyranny of one leader and the instability of a crowd, and expresses the unity of the wider church.

differ.view: Congregational government (Baptist, Congregational, and many independent and free churches)
differ.body: Christ rules each local church directly by his word and Spirit, and under him final earthly authority belongs to the gathered congregation. In the New Testament the whole church receives and disciplines members (Matthew 18:17; 1 Corinthians 5:4-5), chooses the Seven (Acts 6:3-5), joins in the decision of the Jerusalem council (Acts 15:22), and is addressed directly in Paul's letters. The congregation calls its own pastors or elders and deacons, who lead and teach with real authority but remain accountable to the church. Churches cooperate voluntarily in associations but are not governed by them. Defenders argue that this order best honors the priesthood of all believers and the responsibility of every member for the gospel.

Men and women are equal in dignity as bearers of God's image and co-heirs of grace (Genesis 1:27; 1 Peter 3:7), and women serve the church in many essential ways, including in word ministries to other women and children and in some traditions as deacons. But Scripture reserves the office of elder or pastor, with its authority to teach and govern the whole church, to qualified men. Paul grounds his instruction in 1 Timothy 2:12-13 not in local custom but in the order of creation (“For Adam was formed first, and then Eve”), and the qualifications for overseers assume male officeholders (‘husband of one wife’). Jesus chose twelve men as apostles. Defenders include Wayne Grudem, John Piper, and Thomas Schreiner, and they argue that the distinction reflects a good design, not a lesser value.

Men and women are equal in dignity and gifting, and all church offices are open to both according to gift and calling. The Spirit is poured out on sons and daughters who prophesy (Acts 2:17-18); women pray and prophesy in worship (1 Corinthians 11:5); Phoebe was a deacon (Romans 16:1), Priscilla taught Apollos (Acts 18:26), and Junia was “outstanding among the apostles” (Romans 16:7); in the Old Testament Deborah judged Israel and Huldah spoke God's word to the king's officials. Paul's restrictions in 1 Timothy 2 and 1 Corinthians 14 address specific local problems, such as false teaching at Ephesus, and the rare verb authenteō in 1 Timothy 2:12 may mean domineering rather than ordinary authority. Galatians 3:28 states the principle that the gospel works out over time. Defenders include Gordon Fee, Craig Keener, and Philip Payne.

errors:
The church has rejected leadership that treats the flock as property. Ezekiel's shepherds who feed themselves, Jesus' warning against lording it over others, Peter's charge against greed, and John's rebuke of Diotrephes all name the same sin, and church history has repeated it: the buying and selling of church offices (simony), condemned at councils from Chalcedon (451, canon 2) onward; clergy who used their position for wealth, power, or sexual exploitation; and leaders who shielded abusers to protect an institution's reputation. Every tradition teaches that leaders are accountable to Christ, and the New Testament provides for elders who sin to be publicly rebuked (1 Timothy 5:20). The opposite error despises all authority in the church, as if the Spirit's gifts to every believer made ordered leadership unnecessary. Paul answers the disorder at Corinth by insisting that God is “not a God of disorder” (1 Corinthians 14:33), and Hebrews commands believers to follow their leaders.

The church has also rejected the idea that a leader's ordination makes the gospel and sacraments depend on his personal worthiness, the Donatist error, while never excusing unworthy leaders. It has warned against a clericalism that makes ministry the work of a professional class and the congregation its audience, since Ephesians 4 makes leaders equippers of every member. And it has consistently judged that character is the first qualification for office. The lists in 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1 concern almost entirely how a man lives, speaks, and treats his household and neighbors, so that giftedness, charisma, or success can never substitute for a life above reproach.
life:
For those who lead, this doctrine is sobering and freeing. Leaders in the church do not own the people they serve; they will “give an account” (Hebrews 13:17) to the Chief Shepherd, who laid down his life for the flock. That makes pastoral leadership a matter of prayer, patience, and example rather than image or control, and it means the work of the leader is measured by how well the church is equipped to serve, not by how much the leader does himself. It also relieves leaders of the impossible burden of being the church's savior: Moses was told he could not bear the people alone, and Christ gave many gifts to the body so that no one would try.

For those who are led, the doctrine calls for honor, prayer, and trust given to those who teach and watch over them, joined with discernment, since leaders are to be tested and held to the standards Scripture sets. Believers who have been wounded by leaders who abused their position can find in Ezekiel 34 and in Jesus' words a clear judgment that such leaders betrayed the Shepherd they claimed to represent, and the promise that God himself seeks the scattered and binds up the injured. And for every Christian, the pattern of servant leadership applies far beyond church office: in families, workplaces, and communities, those who follow Jesus exercise whatever authority they have as he did, for the good of others and not for themselves.
questions: The New Testament calls the same leaders elders, overseers, and shepherds. What does each title suggest about the work, and how does Ezekiel 34 shape what it means to be a shepherd of God's people?

The qualifications for elders and deacons in 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1 are mostly about character. Why might Scripture place character ahead of gifts or skills, and what happens to a church when that order is reversed?

Christians differ on church government and on women in office. What convictions about leadership do the positions share, and how can churches that disagree on these questions still recognize one another's ministries?
